name: Tara Schmidt

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and we don't sell anything or campaign for any side. Your answers are confidential. What does a normal working day look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I drive the water truck around the large mine to keep dust down on the haul roads. I have a vocational certificate and enough years here to know which bends go powdery before lunch, though my pay is low for an experienced operator. My partner Jules has a steady part-time job at a laundry, and our children are grown. We have less than a month's expenses saved because we used most of the cushion after a plumbing leak. There are few other equipment jobs nearby; I use an AI tool now and then for a manual question, but I wait for a mechanic to check any answer that touches the truck.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew that a little software for forms is fine, provided dust checks still come from the road. The morning wind moves the dust whether a spreadsheet notices or not.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My truck hours probably stay in this mild picture, but Jules and I are already close to the edge after the plumbing bill. I don't feel safe calling this calm just because AI turns out small.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the water route and mark the dry bends after each pass. This month Jules and I would rebuild a one-page bill list, and in the first year I'd raise our low operator rate at the union meeting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel tired of counting the days to payday. I can handle a routine form change; what troubles me is another ordinary house repair.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What did the plumbing leak cost you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The kitchen pipe went behind a wall, so we had to pay for repair and drying. Our grown children offered help, but Jules and I preferred to cover it ourselves.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say at the union meeting?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd bring my rate and years of service on paper. I want a fair operator rate, not a favour for being loud.

say: I would accept simpler **forms** while keeping road dust checks with operators.
I would raise the low **operator rate** with the crew.
think: My truck hours seem secure, but our **thin savings** leave little room for repairs.
My partner’s part-time wage helps, though our **bill pressure** remains.
do: Keep driving the **water route** and marking dry bends.
List household bills and raise the **pay rate** at the union meeting.
feel: I feel **tired** of budgeting around the next ordinary repair.
S0.quote: I want a fair operator rate, not a favour for being loud.
fieldNote: Her existing **plumbing loss** explains the thin cushion and anxiety in the mild scenario.
She treats **dust checks** as physical judgment and uses the union to address low experienced-worker pay.

steps.text: Keep driving the water truck and marking dry haul-road bends
Raise the low operator rate at the next union meeting

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say office AI can help with ordering water and planning routes, but drivers need to report where the dust actually blows. I'd ask the safety committee to check any new route before we call it efficient.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If planners trim a water-truck shift, I could lose hours before robots get near my vehicle. With our savings below a month's bills and only a few local openings, even one lost shift matters.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the supervisor for the planned water-truck hours and take my bend notes to the safety committee. If shifts fell in the first year, Jules and I would pause our weekend trips and I'd check the municipal road depot for a driving vacancy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious, though I can still speak up and look for work. A computer route could save fuel, but it can also miss a dusty entrance until someone complains.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you use the new route tool?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If another driver has tested it safely, I'd try the approved screen with them on a quiet shift. I use AI occasionally, but I won't learn a new route while a loaded truck is bearing down on me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make a depot job possible?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I already hold the heavy-vehicle licence, though the depot rarely advertises. I would apply if it did, because we cannot pay to move away for another mine job.

say: I would ask the **safety committee** to review new routes.
I would tell planners to listen to **dust reports** from drivers.
think: A lost **water-truck shift** would hurt our bills quickly.
Few nearby jobs limit my **escape route** if planning reduces hours.
do: Request forecast **driving hours** and bring bend notes to the safety committee.
Pause weekend trips if hours fall and apply at the **road depot** if it advertises.
feel: I feel **anxious**, but still able to question the route and search locally.
S1.quote: A computer route could save fuel, but it can also miss a dusty entrance until someone complains.
fieldNote: She is open to a **tested route tool**, consistent with her measured approach to technology.
Her immediate **job risk** is fewer driving hours through planning, with a rare road-depot vacancy as backup.

steps.text: Bring recorded dust locations to the mine safety committee
Pause weekend trips if water-truck hours fall
Apply to the municipal road depot if a driving vacancy appears

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell our union branch that thinking AI by 2028 can change planning while water-truck robots arrive around 2031. I want a written plan for the drivers and for dust safety, with time to train if the equipment changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The mine may cut a route early and remove my seat when robots can drive it. I would be 60 at the first date and 63 at the second, and a few weeks of savings cannot carry Jules and me through a long job search here.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take our household bills to the union advice session and ask the mine for a dated water-truck plan. If my shifts were cut in 2028, I'd apply at the road depot and ask the public employment office about paid vehicle-inspection training; in 2029 I'd keep any safe paid truck shifts and stop weekend travel.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm scared enough to think about the rent at night, but I have people to ask for help. A plan has to put a wage at the far end of training, not just hand me a badge.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Jules tonight?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my partner Jules that the plumbing repair has left us too little cash to wait quietly. We would count the bills together, then I would call the union representative before the next shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you apply outside mining?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, for heavy-vehicle driving at the depot if it opens. I know the licence counts there, but I don't know whether a vacancy will appear when I need it.

say: I would demand a written **water-truck plan** and dust-safety checks.
I would explain that planning changes in **2028** precede robots around 2031.
think: I could lose shifts early and my truck seat by **2031**.
Our few weeks of **savings** cannot support a long local job search.
do: Ask the union and mine for a dated **equipment plan**.
Apply to the depot and seek **paid inspection training** if shifts fall.
feel: I feel **frightened at night**, while retaining a plan and people to ask.
S2.quote: A plan has to put a wage at the far end of training, not just hand me a badge.
fieldNote: She expects significant **income loss** and describes nighttime rent worry under the fast timeline.
Her proposed **training** requires paid access through the public employment office.

steps.text: Ask the mine and union for a dated water-truck plan
Apply for heavy-vehicle work at the road depot if mine shifts fall
Enroll in paid vehicle-inspection training if the employment office offers it
Stop weekend travel if water-truck hours are cut

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say thinking AI in 2031 will change the route sheets, with driving robots around 2034. Five years should let the mine test dust coverage in public and let drivers compete fairly for new work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 63 I may still be earning the low mine rate, and at 66 I cannot assume retirement will cover rent. The extra time helps, but it does not create savings by itself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the truck route now and ask the safety committee for annual dust readings along the bends. If the mine offers a paid course on the new controls, I'd take it after a working driver tests the system; in 2032 I'd apply to the road depot, and after robots arrive I'd take paid inspection work if a real post opens.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel watchful. I'd rather test a proven system in daylight than reject it from a distance, but I won't gamble the household on an unposted job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the dust readings show?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They would show whether the proposed route leaves the entrance dry in summer. I can argue from records more clearly than from a complaint about a screen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you judge a training offer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask whether practice is paid and whether the mine has posted inspection jobs. A course without either would cost time that I should spend earning.

say: I would insist on measured **dust coverage** before changing routes.
I would give current drivers fair access to **new work**.
think: Retirement at **66** is uncertain with our current savings.
Five years gives time to prepare but no automatic **financial cushion**.
do: Collect annual **dust readings** and continue paid water-truck shifts.
Take a tested paid **controls course** if offered and apply at the depot.
feel: I feel **watchful**, willing to try a proven system.
S3.quote: A course without either would cost time that I should spend earning.
fieldNote: She ties **training value** to paid practice and posted jobs rather than a general promise.
Her **safety-committee records** give her a concrete way to assess route automation over five years.

steps.text: Collect annual dust readings on the mine haul-road bends
Take paid controls training if the mine offers tested equipment
Apply to the road depot for driving work in 2032

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say thinking AI in 2036 and driving robots around 2039 give the mine a decade to handle its people properly. I would still press for clear retirement figures instead of guessing that everyone can leave at a certain age.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 68 at the first date and 71 at the robot date. I hope to be retired, but the savings are thin today, and I cannot promise what our rent and health costs will be then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep driving safely and bring our pay and bills to a public retirement advice appointment this year. In 2037 I'd compare actual retirement income with rent before reducing shifts; if the numbers failed, I'd ask the depot about paid driving work and keep earning until we could close the gap.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy about money even with a decade to prepare. The technology is distant, but the household budget isn't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ask your children for help?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our children have their own households. I would ask them for advice about a form, perhaps, but I won't build retirement on their wages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What change would ease things sooner?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A fairer mine rate and reliable hours would let Jules and me rebuild savings after the leak. That is a union issue we can work on now, well before a 2039 machine arrives.

say: I would ask for **retirement figures** before assuming older workers can leave.
I would put robot water trucks around **2039**.
think: I hope to retire by **71**, but our thin savings make that uncertain.
Current **rent and health costs** matter more than a distant forecast.
do: Keep safe paid shifts and attend a **retirement advice** appointment.
Compare actual retirement income with **rent** in 2037 before reducing hours.
feel: I feel **uneasy** about current bills despite the long lead time.
S4.quote: The technology is distant, but the household budget isn't.
fieldNote: Her **thin savings** mean a ten-year warning does not remove present financial anxiety.
She seeks **public advice** and continues paid driving until real retirement figures cover living costs.

steps.text: Attend a public retirement advice appointment with pay and bill records
Keep working safe water-truck shifts while income is needed
Ask the road depot for paid driving work if retirement figures fall short

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because our cushion could disappear before a local vacancy appears. Written mine plans, paid training for a real job, and a fair operator rate would make the warning useful.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about dust at the workers' entrance. A clever route that leaves people coughing is not a clever route to me.

headlineQuote: A clever route that leaves people coughing is not a clever route to me.
portrait: Tara is an **experienced water-truck driver** at a large mine, paid below the usual rate for her work.
She and Jules have grown children and less than **one month** of expenses saved after a plumbing leak.
She uses AI **occasionally** and would test a proven route tool with another driver.
She uses **dust records**, union meetings and limited local job searches to protect paid work.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** worries her most because her savings could run out before a local vacancy appears.
whatWouldHelp: She wants a written **equipment plan**, paid job-linked training and a fairer operator rate.
